title: The electron gas
scope: Secs. 2.1 (lattice and jellium, non-interacting, finite T) and 2.2 (first and second order perturbation theory). Excluded: 2.3 (electron gases in 3, 2, 1, 0 dimensions, Eqs. 2.50-2.55); its exercises are used here only as 2D and 1D analogues of Sec. 2.1.2.

keyResults.name: Full electron-ion Hamiltonian
keyResults.note: Eqs. (2.1)-(2.4). Each term is written in second quantization, with no double counting in the electron-ion term.

sections.title: Bloch theory of electrons in a static ion lattice

keyResults.name: Bloch theorem
keyResults.latex: $$\psi_{n\mathbf k\sigma}(\mathbf r)=u_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)\,e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}\chi_\sigma,\qquad u_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r+\mathbf R)=u_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)$$
keyResults.note: Eqs. (2.7)-(2.15). The reciprocal lattice is in Eqs. (2.7)-(2.10), and k is taken in the first Brillouin zone.

keyResults.name: Effective mass approximation
keyResults.latex: $$\psi_{n\mathbf k\sigma}\to e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}\chi_\sigma\ \text{with}\ m\to m^*$$
keyResults.note: Eq. (2.16). Bloch electrons are treated as plane waves with an effective mass.

questions.prompt: In 3D, the Fermi wavenumber in terms of the electron density $n$ (spin 1/2) is
questions.solution: Counting states in $k$ space with spin 2 gives $n=k_F^3/(3\pi^2)$, Eq. (2.26). The option $(6\pi^2 n)^{1/3}$ forgets the spin factor 2.

questions.prompt: Show that $E^{(0)}/N=\tfrac35\varepsilon_F$ for the free electron gas at $T=0$.
questions.solution:
Sum the kinetic energy over the Fermi sphere with spin 2:
$$E^{(0)}=2\frac{\mathcal V}{(2\pi)^3}\int_{k<k_F}4\pi k^2dk\,\frac{\hbar^2k^2}{2m}=\frac{\mathcal V\hbar^2k_F^5}{10\pi^2m}.$$
With $N=\mathcal Vk_F^3/(3\pi^2)$,
$$\frac{E^{(0)}}{N}=\frac{3\hbar^2k_F^2}{10m}=\frac35\cdot\frac{\hbar^2k_F^2}{2m}=\frac35\varepsilon_F.$$

questions.prompt: At small Wigner-Seitz radius $r_s$ (high density) in the jellium gas:
choices: The kinetic energy dominates, because it scales as $r_s^{-2}$ and the Coulomb term scales as $r_s^{-1}$
The kinetic energy dominates, because it scales as $r_s^{2}$
The Coulomb energy dominates, because it scales as $r_s^{-2}$
Neither dominates, because both scale as $r_s^{-1}$
questions.solution: Eq. (2.38) gives $E^{(0)}/N\propto r_s^{-2}$ and Eq. (2.42) gives $E^{(1)}/N\propto r_s^{-1}$. The ratio is $\propto r_s$, so the kinetic term wins at small $r_s$.

questions.prompt: Why is there no direct first-order (Hartree, $q=0$) energy in jellium, and what sign does the exchange term have?
questions.solution:
The $q=0$ Coulomb term is cancelled by the uniform positive background, so the prime in Eq. (2.34) removes it.

The exchange term from Eq. (2.42) is $E^{(1)}/N=-0.916/r_s$ Ry, which is negative. It lowers the energy and binds the gas, because the Pauli principle keeps same-spin electrons apart.

questions.prompt: Derive $k_F$ and the density of states per area $d(\varepsilon)$ for a 2D electron gas, in analogy with Sec. 2.1.2 (Book Exercise 2.4).
questions.solution:
Book Exercise 2.4. With spin 2 and area $A$, the number of states inside a disk of radius $k_F$ is
$$N=2A\frac{\pi k_F^2}{(2\pi)^2}\quad\Rightarrow\quad n=\frac{k_F^2}{2\pi},\qquad k_F=\sqrt{2\pi n}.$$
The energy in terms of $n$ is $\varepsilon=\hbar^2k^2/2m$, so the number of states per area below $\varepsilon$ is
$$n(\varepsilon)=\frac{k^2}{2\pi}=\frac{m\varepsilon}{\pi\hbar^2}.$$
Differentiating gives the density of states per area
$$d(\varepsilon)=\frac{m}{\pi\hbar^2}\,\theta(\varepsilon),$$
which is constant in energy (spin included).

questions.prompt: Same as H1 for a 1D electron gas: find $k_F$ and the density of states per length (Book Exercise 2.5).
questions.solution:
Book Exercise 2.5. With spin 2 and length $L$, the occupied states are $|k|<k_F$, with $k=2\pi n/L$. Then
$$N=2\,L\frac{2k_F}{2\pi}\quad\Rightarrow\quad n=\frac{2k_F}{\pi},\qquad k_F=\frac{\pi n}{2}.$$
The number of states per length below energy $\varepsilon$ is $n(\varepsilon)=\frac{2}{\pi}k(\varepsilon)$ with $k=\sqrt{2m\varepsilon}/\hbar$. Therefore
$$d(\varepsilon)=\frac{dn}{d\varepsilon}=\frac{1}{\pi\hbar}\sqrt{\frac{2m}{\varepsilon}}\,\theta(\varepsilon),$$
which diverges as $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$ at the band edge.

questions.prompt: Minimize the first-order energy $E/N=2.21/r_s^2-0.916/r_s$ Ry to find $r_s^*$ and $E^*/N$, and compare with Na.
questions.solution:
Set $\partial_{r_s}(E/N)=0$:
$$-\frac{2\cdot2.21}{r_s^3}+\frac{0.916}{r_s^2}=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad r_s^*=\frac{2\cdot2.21}{0.916}\approx4.83.$$
At this point
$$\frac{E^*}{N}=\frac{2.21}{r_s^{*2}}-\frac{0.916}{r_s^*}=-\frac{0.916^2}{4\cdot2.21}\approx-0.095\ \text{Ry}\approx-1.29\ \text{eV}.$$
For comparison, the book's experimental value for Na is $r_s=3.96$ and $-0.083$ Ry, which is $-1.13$ eV (Eq. 2.44). The first-order formula at $r_s=3.96$ gives about $-0.090$ Ry, so the approximation is close but not exact.
